lesson.menu_desc: Reading model -- building a pitch: pitch, stakeholder, rationale, evidence, back up, compelling, credibility, track record, outweigh, buy-in -- and connectors of addition and result: in addition, what is more, therefore, as a result -- 29 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 26 -- Persuasion Skills -- Winning the Room
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Simone Quiles de Santana Marques | Lesson 26 -- Persuasion Skills
lesson.grammar_point: connectors of addition and result to build an argument (in addition / furthermore / what is more / therefore / as a result)

listenings.text: Simone, it is Javier Ruiz, from the business team in Madrid. I heard that legal wants three more weeks to review the property files in Campinas, and I need to be honest with you: my stakeholders are not happy. The board wants to close at the end of March, and New York has already accepted that date. So, before Thursday's deal committee, I need a compelling reason, not a list of everything that could go wrong. Tell me your rationale in two sentences. Show me evidence: dates, numbers, documents. And tell me what it costs us if we do not wait. I am not against you. In fact, your team has a good track record, and that gives you credibility with me. But the committee will only give you buy-in if the benefit clearly outweighs the delay. You have five minutes for your pitch. Use them well.

Okay. Five minutes, three parts. Here is my pitch for Thursday. The property files in Campinas have not been checked since two thousand and nineteen. That is my first reason, and I can back it up with the data room index. In addition, the target had a problem with the regulator two years ago, so its track record is not clean. What is more, the antitrust clearance will take about ninety days anyway, so three weeks of review does not move the closing date at all. Therefore, I am asking for three more weeks, with a clear deadline and one person responsible. And the cost of not waiting? If there is a hidden liability in those files, our exposure is the whole value of the deal. The cost of three weeks does not outweigh that. One more thing: I am not going to say the risk is huge. It is not. It is small, but it is serious, and I have the evidence on one page.

extra_audio.text: First, you think about each stakeholder and what they are afraid of losing. Then, you choose one or two clear reasons, and that is your rationale. After that, you find evidence to back up each reason: a date, a number or a document. Next, you add the second reason with in addition, or with what is more. Finally, you finish with the request, as a result of the reasons: therefore, I am asking for it.

paras: Most lawyers believe that a good argument wins by itself. It does not. In a meeting with business people, the best legal reasoning can lose to one simple sentence: we need to close in March. The reason is that the other side is not judging the argument. They are judging the person, the risk, and the cost of saying yes.

A persuasive case has three parts. The first is the rationale: one or two clear reasons, not ten. The second is the evidence that backs up each reason: a date, a number, a document. The third is the request, and it should come at the end, as the result of the reasons. In addition, the order matters. If you start with the request, people stop listening and start defending.

Credibility is the part nobody sees. A lawyer with a good track record can make a short pitch and win. A lawyer who has exaggerated risks in the past needs much more evidence for the same result. Therefore, never call a risk huge when it is moderate. One exaggeration costs more than one lost argument.

Finally, think about the stakeholders before the meeting, not during it. Ask what each person is afraid of losing. A business director is usually afraid of losing time; a finance director is afraid of losing money. If your plan protects what they are afraid of, the benefit outweighs the cost, and you get real buy-in instead of a polite yes.

reading.prompt: Read once, quickly. Which title fits the whole text best?
choices: Lawyers should always open the meeting with their request, because business people have very little time for long explanations
A good argument needs clear reasons, evidence, credibility and attention to each stakeholder
Why business directors never accept legal arguments

items: The text says a good legal argument usually wins by itself.
It does not: business people judge the person, the risk and the cost of saying yes.
According to the text, the request should come at the end.
It comes as the result of the reasons; if you start with it, people start defending.
A lawyer with a good track record needs more evidence than other lawyers.
The opposite: a good track record lets you make a short pitch and win.
The text says one exaggeration can cost you more than one lost argument.
Never call a risk huge when it is moderate: you lose credibility.
According to the text, a finance director is usually most afraid of losing time.
That is the business director. The finance director is usually afraid of losing money.
